Self-sufficiency gives a remote motive for disregarding a shared divine boundary, without a direct route.
It condemns preventing Allah's name from being remembered in His mosques and striving to ruin them, a direct access-obstruction parallel.
It commands orientation toward the Sacred Mosque, establishing it as the shared qiblah later reiterated in the listed verses.
Safa and Marwah are Allah's rites for pilgrimage and visitation, extending the focus's sanctuary into its ritual access network.
The sacred month and reciprocal limits on violation clarify that protected time and place constrain response to aggression.
It regulates completing Hajj and Umrah for Allah, including impediment and sacrificial release, directly framing lawful access to the sanctuary.
The first House established for people at Bakkah grounds the focus's Sacred Mosque in a public, blessed place.
The House is a secure sanctuary for people and pilgrimage to it is imposed on those able, closely supporting shared access and inviolability.
Its prohibition and expiation rules while in pilgrimage clarify that sacred access carries enforceable limits on conduct.
The pilgrimage state distinguishes permitted provision from prohibited land hunting, supplying another protected-boundary rule.
It identifies the opponents' corrupt ritual at the House, qualifying claims to occupy or control the sanctuary.
It denies that idolaters may maintain Allah's mosques while bearing witness against themselves by disbelief.
It defines legitimate maintenance of Allah's mosques through faith, worship, almsgiving, and fear of Allah alone.
Abraham asks that the city be made secure and that he and his descendants be kept from idolatry, directly joining sanctuary and protection.
The call to pilgrimage brings people on foot and by lean mount to the House, materially extending its equal availability to distant visitors.
Pilgrims are summoned to witness benefits and invoke Allah over provision, supplying the communal purpose of access to the sacred precinct.
Its instructions to complete rites, fulfill vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House specify lawful use of the sanctuary.
Honoring Allah's sacred ordinances establishes the governing norm that the focus's wrongful intent violates.
Venerating Allah's rites is identified as a matter of piety, reinforcing the protected status at issue in 22:25.
The rites and sacrificial animals have an appointed place of offering at the Ancient House, extending the sanctuary's regulated use.
Sacrificial animals are Allah's rites and their offering is governed by divine instruction, adding the ritual dimension of the sacred precinct.
It calls Makkah a secure sanctuary to which provisions are brought, directly connecting protected place, public safety, and livelihood.
It contrasts the secure sanctuary with insecurity around it and condemns disbelief in that divine provision.
Those who commit ilhad regarding Allah's signs are contrasted with those who come securely, providing the closest additional use of the focus's deviation term.
It situates divine restraint of conflict in the valley of Makkah after victory, showing the sacred locality as a protected limit on violence.
It promises secure entry into the Sacred Mosque with heads shaved or hair shortened and without fear, directly completing the access theme.
Worship of the Lord of this House supplies the House's theological center, though not its access rule.
Security from fear and provision after hunger give the House's surrounding sanctuary its social purpose.
